pos: n. pl. (the twelve signs; the constellations of the zodiac)
etymology: Hebrew mazzalah, the constellations or signs of the zodiac, from a root meaning to distribute or apportion. The Authorized Version's planets uses the older English sense of wandering stars, and the context is the astral religion Josiah destroyed.
biblical_def: And he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places round about Jerusalem; them also that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the host of heaven. This is Josiah's reformation, and the catalogue shows how deep the rot had gone. These were not foreign priests; the kings of Judah had ordained them, giving astral worship an official establishment inside the covenant nation. The list ascends from Baal through sun and moon and signs to all the host of heaven, which is the Bible's standing phrase for the created lights worshipped as powers. Moses had forbidden it in terms that name both the attraction and the answer: lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven. The stars are real, they are beautiful, and they are creatures — distributed by God to everyone alike, and therefore no one's god. The LORD presses the same point to Job by asking whether he can bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion. Josiah's reform reached further than the altars: the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land did Josiah put away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a celestial body which revolves about the sun; a wandering star, as distinguished from the fixed stars.
webster_full: PLANET, n. A celestial body which revolves about the sun or other center, or a body revolving about another planet.
PLANET, n. The primary planets are so called because they appear to wander among the fixed stars.
PLANETARY, a. Pertaining to the planets; consisting of planets; under the dominion of a planet, in the language of astrologers.
ZODIAC, n. A broad circle in the heavens, containing the twelve signs through which the sun passes in its annual course.
HOST, n. The whole army of heaven; the celestial bodies; also, the angels.
scriptures: 2 Kings 23:5

And he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places round about Jerusalem; them also that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the host of heaven.
Deuteronomy 4:19

And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven.
Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?
2 Kings 23:24

Moreover the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away, that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Astrology is treated as harmless entertainment and has been absorbed into ordinary speech and self-description; Scripture classes it among the abominations a reforming king tore out of the land.
corruption_paragraphs: Star-signs have re-entered common life so thoroughly that they no longer look religious. People who would never call themselves worshippers of the host of heaven nonetheless identify by a sign, consult a horoscope, and explain their temperament by a birth date. Scripture's category for this is not superstition but idolatry, because it assigns to creatures a government over human life that belongs to the Creator. Josiah did not negotiate with it; the text says he put down the priests, and the sweep of verse 24 shows the reform was total. A practice does not become innocent by ceasing to feel serious.

There is a second and sharper observation in the passage. The astral priests had been ordained by the kings of Judah. This was not folk religion at the margins but an establishment maintained by the covenant nation's own leadership, standing alongside the temple. That is how syncretism always arrives: not as a rival announcing itself, but as an addition quietly given official standing until it is simply part of how things are done. The test Scripture applies is the regulative one — God has said how he will be worshipped, and what he has not commanded is not permitted. The book found in the house of the LORD is what exposed the whole arrangement, which is the usual way such things are exposed.
roots_summary: Hebrew mazzalah (H4208), the signs of the zodiac; tsaba hashamayim (H6635), the host of heaven; kemarim (H3649), idolatrous priests; qatar (H6999), to burn incense.

“whom the kings of Judah had ordained” — an official establishment.
“canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades?” — the stars as creatures.

pos: n. (carved or painted figures; a chamber of images)
etymology: Hebrew maskith, a carved figure or ornamented device, from a root meaning to show or display. The Authorized Version's chambers of his imagery renders a phrase for private rooms whose walls carried idolatrous carvings.
biblical_def: Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth. Ezekiel has been brought in vision to the temple and shown what is happening inside it. He had dug through a wall and gone in, and what he found is described in the preceding verses: every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, pourtrayed upon the wall round about. The men doing this are the ancients — the elders, the responsible leadership of the covenant people — and they are doing it in the dark, each in his own chamber. Two things make the passage devastating. The idolatry is concealed and personal; every man has a room of his own. And the reasoning behind it is quoted: the LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth. They have not stopped believing in God; they have concluded he is absent, and absence is all that secret sin requires. The vision continues upward through worse abominations to men at the very door of the temple with their backs toward the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east, worshipping the sun. And the chapter ends with God's answer to the reasoning: therefore will I also deal in fury: mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): sensible representations, pictures, statues; forms of the fancy; false ideas; imaginary phantasms.
webster_full: IMAGERY, n. Sensible representations, pictures, statues.
IMAGERY, n. Forms of the fancy; false ideas; imaginary phantasms.
IMAGERY, n. Representations in writing or speaking; lively descriptions which impress the images of things on the mind.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; a picture.
CHAMBER, n. An apartment in an upper story, or in a story above the lower floor of a dwelling house; a retired or private place.
scriptures: Ezekiel 8:12

Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth.
Ezekiel 8:10
So I went in and saw; and behold every form of creeping things, and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel, pourtrayed upon the wall round about.
Ezekiel 8:16

And he brought me into the inner court of the LORD'S house, and, behold, at the door of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about five and twenty men, with their backs toward the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east.
Ezekiel 8:18
Therefore will I also deal in fury: mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: and though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them.
corruption_summary: Private sin is regarded as nobody's business and as lighter because unseen; Ezekiel shows leaders reasoning exactly that way, and God answering that the darkness changes nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Every man in the chamber of his imagery is an unnervingly apt description of the age. The images are now carried rather than carved, the chamber is a screen, and the privacy is far more complete than any elder of Israel could have arranged — but the structure is identical: a private room, filled with images, entered in the dark, by men who hold office and would be appalled to be seen. The reasoning is identical too, though it is rarely spoken aloud. The LORD seeth us not is the operative premise of all secret sin, and it need not be believed theologically to be relied on practically. Psalm 139 is the standing answer, and Ezekiel 8 is its illustration: God brought a prophet through the wall to look.

The second matter is who is doing this. The ancients of the house of Israel — the elders, the men charged with the spiritual oversight of the nation. Scripture is consistent in locating the worst corruption nearest the sanctuary, and Ezekiel's vision moves inward and upward through escalating abominations until it arrives at men standing between the porch and the altar with their backs to the temple. That is the picture of a leadership that has kept its position and reversed its direction. The church's qualifications for eldership are weighted toward character rather than ability for precisely this reason, and the passage is a standing argument against treating a leader's private life as a separate question from his office.

“the LORD seeth us not” — the premise of all secret sin.
“their backs toward the temple of the LORD” — position kept, direction reversed.

pos: n. pl. (tombs; vaults where the dead are laid)
etymology: Hebrew natsar, to watch or guard, in a form meaning secret or guarded places — here, tombs. Latin monumentum, a memorial, from monere, to remind. The biblical sense is sepulchral: a place of the dead, not a public statue.
biblical_def: Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels. Isaiah is describing a people practising forbidden rites, and every detail is a deliberate crossing of a line God had drawn. They remain among the graves and lodge in the monuments — spending nights in tombs, a practice associated with necromancy and with seeking dreams or oracles from the dead. They eat swine's flesh, expressly unclean under the law. Their vessels hold the broth of abominable things. This is not ignorance but deliberate transgression by people who know the law, and the LORD's summary of them is given in the verses before: a people that provoketh me to anger continually to my face; that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick. The phrase to my face is the heart of the indictment. The corruption is not indifference but defiance. And the passage begins with one of the most affecting descriptions of God in Scripture, which makes the defiance worse rather than better: I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts. The outstretched hands and the tomb-lodging stand in the same paragraph, and Paul quotes that first line in Romans and applies it to Israel in his own day.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): anything by which the memory of a person or event is preserved; a tomb; a sepulchral structure.
webster_full: MONUMENT, n. Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated; a building, stone, or other thing placed or erected to remind men of the person who raised it.
MONUMENT, n. A tomb; a cenotaph; a place where the dead body of a person is deposited.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; a place in which the body of a deceased person is laid.
ABOMINABLE, a. Very hateful; detestable; loathsome; unclean; in the Mosaic law, that which was forbidden as unclean.
NECROMANCY, n. The art of revealing future events by means of a pretended communication with the dead.
scriptures: Isaiah 65:4
Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
Isaiah 65:3
A people that provoketh me to anger continually to my face; that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick;
Isaiah 65:2
I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts;
Leviticus 19:31
Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God.
corruption_summary: Traffic with the dead is presented as comfort or as cultural practice, and rebellion is explained as ignorance; Isaiah describes people who know the law and provoke God to his face.
corruption_paragraphs: Seeking the dead has always been marketed as consolation, and it still is — the medium who brings a message from a lost parent, the ritual that maintains contact, the practice defended as a way of honouring someone. Scripture's prohibition is absolute and its reason is given: to be defiled by them. The defilement is in the seeking. The Bible offers real comfort concerning the dead and it comes from the opposite direction — not word from them but the promise of resurrection, so that believers sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. The tombs of Isaiah 65 are a counterfeit of that hope, and they defile.

The harder word in the passage concerns motive. Modern readings of Old Testament apostasy tend toward the sympathetic: the people were poorly taught, the culture pressed on them, the practices were simply what everyone did. Isaiah gives a different account — continually to my face — and sets it against God's hands spread out all the day. That is defiance, not confusion, and the seriousness of the biblical doctrine of sin depends on the distinction. A God whose hands are stretched out all day long is not being misunderstood by the people lodging in the tombs; he is being refused.

roots_lines: Hebrew natsar (H5341) — to watch, to keep; in this form, secret or guarded places; rendered monuments.

Hebrew piggul (H6292) — refuse, foul flesh; broth of abominable things.

“provoketh me to anger continually to my face” — defiance, not ignorance.
“I have spread out my hands all the day” — what the defiance answers.

pos: n. pl. (illicit lovers; those loved outside a covenant)
etymology: Hebrew pilegesh, a concubine, here used with deliberate coarseness of illicit partners. The English comes from Old French par amour, by way of love — a phrase that once meant devotion and hardened into a word for an unlawful lover.
biblical_def: For she doted upon their paramours, whose flesh is as the flesh of asses, and whose issue is like the issue of horses. Ezekiel 23 is the most deliberately offensive chapter in Scripture, and the offence is the argument. God depicts Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters who became prostitutes, and the language grows steadily coarser as the chapter proceeds, refusing every opportunity to soften. The reason is that the subject is not sexual sin but covenant treachery, and God is determined that his people feel about their idolatry what they would feel about this. The relationships in view are Judah's alliances with Egypt and Assyria — political and religious entanglements pursued for security — and doted is the word for an infatuation that has lost its judgment. Ezekiel traces the habit back to its origin: she multiplied her whoredoms, in calling to remembrance the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt. And God states the actual charge at the end of the chapter in plain terms, stripped of the figure: because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms. The whole chapter rests on a prior reality established in Ezekiel 16 — I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine. There can be no adultery without a marriage first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a lover; one who loves; formerly used of either sex; now, one who loves or is loved illicitly.
webster_full: PARAMOUR, n. A lover; one who loves or is beloved.
PARAMOUR, n. A mistress; one who is loved and courted unlawfully.
DOTE, v.i. To love to excess; to be foolishly fond; to regard with excessive and often unreasoning affection.
CONCUBINE, n. A woman who cohabits with a man, without the authority of a legal marriage.
WHOREDOM, n. The practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex; in Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God.
scriptures: Ezekiel 23:20
For she doted upon their paramours, whose flesh is as the flesh of asses, and whose issue is like the issue of horses.
Ezekiel 23:19
Yet she multiplied her whoredoms, in calling to remembrance the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt.
Ezekiel 23:35
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms.
Ezekiel 16:8

Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.
corruption_summary: The chapter is either treated as an embarrassment to be skipped or read as evidence that Scripture degrades women; it is a covenant lawsuit in which God uses the most painful analogy available to describe what idolatry does to him.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection to Ezekiel 23 is that its imagery is violent and its figures female, and it is read as a text that demeans women. The reading mistakes the referents. The two sisters are Samaria and Jerusalem — two political and religious entities, populated overwhelmingly by men, whose kings and priests and elders made the alliances being described. The figure is chosen not because women are especially prone to unfaithfulness but because marriage is the covenant God chose to describe his bond with his people, and adultery is therefore the only analogy adequate to their treachery. The men who ran the nation are the adulteress in the parable.

The churchly failure is simple avoidance. Chapters like this are skipped in preaching, and the omission costs something specific: the felt weight of what idolatry is. Ezekiel is not being gratuitous; he is refusing to let a covenant people describe their spiritual condition in language mild enough to live with. The flat statement at the end of the chapter is the key to the whole — thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back. God speaks of himself here as a betrayed husband, which is a claim about his love before it is a claim about their sin, and a church that cannot bear the chapter has not understood what it is being told about God.

pos: v. (to give over to unlawful use; to expose for hire)
etymology: Hebrew chalal, to profane, to make common — the same verb used of profaning the sabbath and the sanctuary. Latin prostituere, to set forth in public, to expose for sale. The Hebrew is the more revealing: to prostitute is to make common what was holy.
biblical_def: Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness. The command is addressed to fathers, and the Hebrew verb is the key to it. Chalal means to profane — to take something set apart and make it common. Scripture's objection to this trade is therefore not squeamishness about the body but the desecration of a person made in God's image and entrusted to a father's protection. The cultic background is real: the surrounding nations attached prostitution to their temples, and Israel is forbidden it in those terms as well — there shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel. The reason given in the verse deserves attention because it runs against the modern instinct entirely. The prohibition is grounded not only in the harm to the daughter but in what it does to the nation: lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness. Scripture assumes that private transactions have public consequences and that a land can be defiled by what its households permit. Sexual sin in the Bible is never merely a matter between consenting parties, and the law addresses the man with the power, which here is the father who could sell his own child.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to offer to a lewd use, or to indiscriminate lewdness; to devote to any base purpose; to give up to a low use.
webster_full: PROSTITUTE, v.t. To offer freely to a lewd use, or to indiscriminate lewdness.
PROSTITUTE, v.t. To devote to any thing base; to give up to any vile purpose; as, to prostitute talents to the propagation of vice.
PROSTITUTE, n. A female given to indiscriminate lewdness; a strumpet.
PROFANE, v.t. To violate any thing sacred, or treat it with abuse, irreverence or contempt; to put to a wrong or unworthy use.
WHOREDOM, n. The practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex; in Scripture, idolatry.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:29
Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness.
Deuteronomy 23:17
There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel.
Hebrews 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Ezekiel 16:8

Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.
corruption_summary: The trade is relabelled as work freely chosen between consenting adults, and its industrialised form is consumed privately at enormous scale; Scripture calls it profaning a person and holds that a land is defiled by it.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary case rests on consent and autonomy: what adults agree to is nobody else's concern, and the trade is best understood as labour deserving recognition rather than prohibition. Leviticus 19:29 denies both premises. The Hebrew verb says a person is being profaned, which is language of desecration rather than of contract, and the consequence named is public — lest the land fall to whoredom. Consent does not undo desecration; a man may agree to his own degradation and it remains degradation. The dictionary also notes what the verse assumes about the people involved: the daughter here is being disposed of by someone with power over her, which remains the ordinary shape of the trade in every century.

Pornography is this text's most obvious modern application and the one most often evaded, since no transaction appears to occur in the viewer's room. The trade is nonetheless there, industrialised, with real persons profaned at its source. And the corruption Leviticus warns of — a land grown full of wickedness — describes the downstream effects with uncomfortable accuracy: marriages hollowed, appetites trained toward what Scripture forbids, a generation catechised in a false account of the body. Against all of it Scripture sets not prudery but a high doctrine of the body and of marriage: marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled.

Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — a wicked purpose, lewdness; rendered wickedness.

pos: n. (the married state; the bond of marriage)
etymology: Old English wedlac, from wed, a pledge, and -lac, an action or offering — literally the giving of a pledge. It is not lock, despite appearances, though the folk sense of a binding has attached itself to the word.
biblical_def: And I will judge thee, as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged; and I will give thee blood in fury and jealousy. God is speaking to Jerusalem under the figure of an unfaithful wife, and the sentence has a legal shape: she will be judged by the standard applied to women who break wedlock. Behind the judgment stands the covenant that makes it possible, described earlier in the same chapter in language of extraordinary tenderness — I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine. The wedlock is real; that is why its breaking is adultery rather than mere disloyalty. Ezekiel then presses the comparison to its most painful point, noting that this wife is worse than an ordinary adulteress because she takes strangers instead of her husband while receiving gifts rather than payment. The word jealousy in the verse is not a defect in God but the necessary form of covenant love: a husband who is indifferent to his wife's adultery does not love her. This is why Scripture uses marriage as its master figure for the relation between God and his people from Sinai to the marriage supper of the Lamb, and why the New Testament guards actual marriage so firmly: marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): marriage; matrimony; the state of being married.
webster_full: WEDLOCK, n. Marriage; matrimony; the legal union of a man and woman for life.
WEDLOCK, v.t. To marry; to unite in marriage.
WED, v.t. To marry; to take for husband or for wife; to unite in the most intimate connection.
MATRIMONY, n. Marriage; wedlock; the union of man and woman for life; the nuptial state.
JEALOUSY, n. Suspicious fear or apprehension; in scripture, the vigilance of a covenant love which will not endure a rival.
scriptures: Ezekiel 16:38
And I will judge thee, as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged; and I will give thee blood in fury and jealousy.
Ezekiel 16:8

Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.
Ezekiel 16:32
But as a wife that committeth adultery, which taketh strangers instead of her husband!
Hebrews 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: Marriage has been redefined as a contract between any two persons, terminable at will and detached from permanence, sex, and children; Scripture makes it a covenant before God and the very figure of his bond with his people.
corruption_paragraphs: The legal and cultural redefinition of marriage proceeded in stages, and each stage assumed the previous one. No-fault divorce made the bond terminable and so contractual rather than covenantal. The separation of marriage from childbearing made it a private arrangement for adult satisfaction. The redefinition of the parties followed naturally, because a terminable private arrangement for adult satisfaction has no principled reason to be one man and one woman. Scripture's marriage is fixed at creation and confirmed by Christ: he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, and said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh. The dictionary holds that and does not regard the matter as open.

The theological cost of losing wedlock is larger than the social cost, and it is felt in how the gospel can be told. God chose marriage as the figure for his covenant — Israel as his wife, the church as the bride of Christ, the last vision of Scripture a marriage supper. That figure only communicates in a culture that still knows what a covenant is: a pledge that binds because it was sworn, not because it continues to satisfy. Where marriage has become terminable, Ezekiel 16 becomes unreadable and Ephesians 5 sounds like a metaphor drawn from nothing. Christian households that keep their vows are preserving the vocabulary in which the gospel is preached.

pos: n. (an assessment laid on persons or property)
etymology: Hebrew erek, an estimate or valuation, from arak, to set in order or appraise — the assessed rating of a man's worth for the levy. Latin taxatio, a valuing, from taxare, to appraise.
biblical_def: And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaohnechoh. The verse sits immediately after the death of Josiah and the end of his reformation, and the contrast is deliberate. Josiah had torn out the idols and kept the law; his son pays tribute to Egypt and raises it from his own people. The mechanism is described exactly: an assessment was set on every man, and the money was exacted. Scripture does not condemn taxation as such — the Lord told his hearers to render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and Paul commands Christians to pay tribute to whom tribute is due. What this passage exposes is a particular arrangement: a king raising money from his own people to purchase the favour of a foreign power that had conquered them. Jehoiakim had no independence to protect and no reform to fund. The judgment on him is given in the chapter's framing, since the writer of Kings keeps his own accounts and records that Jehoiakim did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD. The verse is a small, precise portrait of what follows a reformation when the next generation does not hold it: the outward machinery of the state continues, and its burden falls where it always falls.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of laying a tax, or of imposing taxes on the subjects of a state; the sum imposed; a rate or assessment.
webster_full: TAXATION, n. The act of laying a tax, or of imposing taxes on the subjects of a state by government.
TAXATION, n. Tax; sum imposed; the rate or assessment laid on a person or estate.
TAX, n. A rate or sum of money assessed on the person or property of a citizen by government, for the use of the nation or state.
EXACT, v.t. To force or compel to pay or yield; to demand or require authoritatively.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another, either for peace or protection.
scriptures: 2 Kings 23:35

And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaohnechoh.
2 Kings 23:25

And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him.
2 Kings 23:24

Moreover the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away, that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the LORD.
Luke 2:1
And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.
corruption_summary: Scripture is recruited for whichever fiscal politics a reader already holds; what the Bible actually supplies is a doctrine of spheres, a command to pay what is owed, and a standing warning about rulers who exact from their own.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is to make the Bible a partisan document on tax policy in either direction. It will not serve. The Lord commanded the rendering of Caesar's coin to Caesar, and Paul commands tribute, custom, fear, and honour to whom they are due — under a pagan empire, with no suggestion that its rates required Christian approval first. Scripture equally records prophets denouncing rulers who devour their people and a king whose exactions are set down as part of his indictment. The principle to recover is the doctrine of spheres: family, church, and state each have authority God has given and limits God has set, and a state that swells past its sphere is a biblical concern whatever the rate.

The second thing this verse teaches is about generations. Josiah's reformation was thorough — the writer says there was no king like him before or after — and it did not survive his son. The idols came back, the tribute was paid, and the people bore it. Reformation is never inherited. Every generation receives the outward forms and must be brought to the thing itself, which is why Scripture places such weight on households teaching children and why the found book in the house of the LORD is the hinge of Josiah's whole reign. What is not taught afresh is lost, and what follows the loss is usually described in the flat administrative language of this verse.

pos: n. (a market; a place of trade)
etymology: Hebrew sachar, traffic or merchandise, from a root meaning to travel about as a trader. The English mart is a contraction of market, from Latin mercatus, trade. The word occurs once, of Tyre.
biblical_def: And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations. Isaiah is pronouncing judgment on Tyre, the great Phoenician port, and the description is admiring before it is condemning. Tyre really was the mart of nations — grain from the Nile, goods from every coast, a trading city of extraordinary reach and wealth. Scripture does not condemn trade; the description here is factual, Proverbs praises the virtuous woman who perceiveth that her merchandise is good, and the law protects honest weights and measures. What Isaiah names as the offence is stated precisely two verses on: the LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth. The problem is the pride, and the mechanism by which commerce produces it is given in the phrase whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth. In Tyre, trade had become the source of rank. Wealth conferred honour, honour conferred authority, and the city came to regard its position as its own achievement. The same portrait returns at the end of the Bible, where the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over fallen Babylon because no man buyeth their merchandise any more, and the list of her cargo ends with slaves, and souls of men. That is where a mart of nations arrives when nothing restrains it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a place of public traffic; a market; bargain; purchase and sale.
webster_full: MART, n. A place of public traffic or sale; contracted from market.
MART, n. Bargain; purchase and sale.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
TRAFFIC, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling; commodities of trade.
REVENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property; income.
scriptures: Isaiah 23:3
And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations.
Isaiah 23:8
Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?
Isaiah 23:9
The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.
Revelation 18:11
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
corruption_summary: Commerce is defended as morally neutral or condemned as inherently exploitative; Scripture honours honest trade and names the specific corruption — wealth becoming the source of rank and the ground of pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet on passages like this. The first treats markets as a morally neutral mechanism, so that Isaiah's and Ezekiel's long denunciations of Tyre become quaint. The second treats commerce itself as the sin, which requires ignoring the considerable body of Scripture that assumes trade, protects property, honours diligence, and condemns theft. The text is more precise than either. Tyre's offence is that her merchants are princes — the city's ranking order has been set by wealth, and its glory is its own. The Lord's stated purpose is to stain the pride, not to abolish the harbour.

The specific temptation for the Christian is that this corruption is almost invisible from inside it. A trading people does not announce that money has become the measure of a man; it simply arranges its seating that way, in the boardroom and eventually in the pew. James addresses precisely this — a congregation seating the man with the gold ring well and the poor man badly — and calls it being judges of evil thoughts. Revelation's cargo list ends with slaves, and souls of men, which is the terminus: a market with no restraint above it will eventually price people. The remedy Scripture gives is not the abolition of the mart but a fear of God high enough to keep it in its place.

pos: n. pl. (small portable temples or cases for an idol)
etymology: Greek naos, a temple or shrine — here in miniature, the silver models of Diana's temple sold to pilgrims at Ephesus. Latin scrinium, a case or chest for keeping something precious.
biblical_def: For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen. The riot at Ephesus is the clearest case in Scripture of the economics of idolatry, and Luke records the motive without editorial comment because Demetrius states it himself. The silver shrines were souvenir models of the temple of Diana, sold to pilgrims, and the trade was substantial. What triggered the riot was not a theological objection but a commercial one, and Demetrius is candid with his fellow tradesmen about what Paul is doing to the market: ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands. That last clause is the whole apostolic argument in a line, and it is the same argument the prophets made — an idol is manufactured, and what a man makes cannot be his god. The response is the one that greets that argument everywhere: when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians. Two hours of shouting a slogan is what the craft could muster against a sentence of reasoning. The episode is instructive about how idolatry actually defends itself — not by argument, but by volume, and with a financial interest underneath that nobody in the crowd was told about.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a case, box or repository in which sacred things are deposited; an altar or a place hallowed from its associations.
webster_full: SHRINE, n. A case, box or repository in which sacred things are deposited; as the shrines of idols.
SHRINE, n. An altar; a place or object hallowed from its history or associations.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
SILVERSMITH, n. One whose occupation is to work in silver, or to manufacture silver utensils.
CRAFT, n. Manual art; trade; the occupation or employment which requires skill of hand.
scriptures: Acts 19:24
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;
Acts 19:26
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:
Acts 19:28
And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.
Psalm 115:4
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as sincere if mistaken devotion; Acts 19 shows an industry with a payroll defending its market, and the opposition to the gospel following the money.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's account is unsentimental about why cities resist the gospel. Demetrius did not convene his colleagues over a point of theology; he convened them because a preacher was reducing demand for silver shrines. Religion in Ephesus was an economy, with craftsmen, suppliers, and a pilgrim trade attached to the temple, and a message that idols made with hands are no gods threatened all of it. The pattern recurs wherever a system has revenue attached. Opposition to Christian truth is regularly framed in principled terms by people whose livelihood depends on the principle, and Scripture is willing to say so plainly.

The second observation concerns how the crowd answered. Paul's claim was an argument, stated in one sentence and reported by his opponent: they be no gods, which are made with hands. It admits of a reply, and none was offered. What came instead was two hours of a chanted slogan, and Luke notes drily a few verses later that the more part knew not wherefore they were come together. That is the ordinary shape of resistance to the gospel in any century — not counter-argument but volume, assertion, and a crowd that has not been told what the meeting is about. The church's response then and now is the same: keep making the argument, and keep it about who God is.

pos: n. (a shelter of foliage; a covering that shades)
etymology: Hebrew choresh, a wood or thicket — here the dense canopy of a great tree. Old English scrud, a garment or covering. The now-dominant sense of a burial cloth is later English; the biblical use is arboreal.
biblical_def: Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs. Ezekiel is warning Pharaoh by describing what happened to somebody greater, and the figure is a magnificent tree. The shroud is its canopy — the shadowing cover of foliage that made it a shelter for everything beneath. The prophet develops that shelter at length and generously: all the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations. Assyria genuinely did provide order and protection over a vast territory, and Ezekiel says so. Then he names the fault, and it is one word: height. Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height — therefore the sentence follows. The tree is given into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen and cut down. Nothing in the passage condemns greatness as such; God made the tree, and the chapter says elsewhere that he made it fair. What is condemned is a greatness that has become conscious of itself, in which the heart rises with the stature. Nebuchadnezzar, who is the intended audience of the warning through Pharaoh, later supplied the line that says it perfectly: Is not this great Babylon, that I have built by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which clothes, covers or conceals; shelter; a cover; the dress of the dead; a branch or covering of foliage.
webster_full: SHROUD, n. That which clothes, covers, conceals or protects; a garment; shelter; cover.
SHROUD, n. The dress of the dead; a winding sheet.
SHROUD, n. A branch of a tree; hence, a covering or shelter of foliage.
CANOPY, n. A covering over a throne, or over a bed; a covering spread over the head.
STATURE, n. The natural height of an animal body; bulk; size; eminence.
scriptures: Ezekiel 31:3
Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches, and with a shadowing shroud, and of an high stature; and his top was among the thick boughs.
Ezekiel 31:6
All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs, and under his branches did all the beasts of the field bring forth their young, and under his shadow dwelt all great nations.
Ezekiel 31:10
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height, and he hath shot up his top among the thick boughs, and his heart is lifted up in his height;
Daniel 4:30
The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
corruption_summary: National and personal greatness is treated as self-generated achievement; Ezekiel grants the greatness, credits God with it, and identifies the fall with a heart lifted up in its own height.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is uncontested; the principle to recover is Ezekiel's diagnosis of how great powers fall. Modern accounts of imperial decline reach for economics, overextension, or internal division, and those things are real second causes that Scripture nowhere denies. But Ezekiel places the decisive fault in the heart of the thing: his heart is lifted up in his height. That is a claim about providence — that God raises and casts down nations, and that pride is the condition under which he casts them down. Daniel says the same in plain doctrine: the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.

The passage is also notably generous, which is what makes it useful rather than merely severe. Ezekiel does not pretend Assyria was worthless. The tree was fair, the canopy really did shelter nations, and the birds and beasts really did live under it. Christians commenting on their own nation, institution, or work would do well to imitate the balance. It is possible to acknowledge genuine good achieved under a power that God is about to humble, and Scripture does it in the same paragraph as the sentence. What is not possible is to keep the greatness and lose the ascription. The moment a man says the might of my power and the honour of my majesty, the tree is already marked.
